newsitem.title: UK: French bonds' outperformance of Bunds seen over.
newsitem.headline: French bonds' outperformance of Bunds seen over.

text.p: French employment data released on Friday posed more questions on the state of the nation's economy than they answered, analysts said.
Although the question of whether the economy has turned the corner remains opaque, the message for holders of French bonds is clear: OATs' outperformance of Bunds has run its course.
"The short term risk isn't great, but I can't see the spread over German Bunds going further in their favour," said Gwyn Hacche, international economist at HSBC-James Capel in London.
"All they have to look forward to is the likelihood of a rise in bond volatility and doubts resurfacing over monetary union," Hacche said.
French data released earlier showed unemployment fell by 29,000 in December, or 0.9 percent. However, the jobless rate stayed unchanged at a record 12.7 percent.
Analysts said the figures were unlikely to prompt the Bank of France to make a further cut in the intervention rate, which it trimmed by five basis points to 3.10 percent on Thursday.

"Unemployment may still threaten 13 percent," said Iain Lindsay, senior bond analyst at Credit Lyonnais in Paris. "In terms of policy, the Bank of France doesn't see what it can do about this. From their point of view, it's a structural problem."

Benchmark 10-year OATs yield 5.61 percent, 17 basis points less than comparable German Bunds which yield 5.78 percent. That compares with a spread where French bonds yielded more than 50 basis points over Germany a year ago.

Hacche said most of French bonds' (OATs) outperformance of the German Bund market was pegged to expectations that European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) would go ahead on time, and with France as a core member.

Some analysts are concerned that since so much good news and optimism is already priced into European bond markets -- as the sharp narrowing of Spanish and Italian spreads testifies -- an unwinding of that optimism is inevitable.
By the end of 1997, on the assumption that a delay to EMU from its start date of January 1999 will be on the cards, Hacche said the OAT/Bund spread will head back to 50 basis points.
Even the prospect of further lowering in the intervention rate, to match the German repo rate, is unlikely to tempt investors into buying French paper.

"They're already in striking distance, and another 10 basis points is academic," said Lindsay. He added that French and German money market rates were already comparable and such monetary fine-tuning would not make much difference.
He said he had seen an increasing number of German and Austrian accounts closing their positions in French debt assets completely -- purely on the basis of yield consideration.
French domestic investors were uncomfortable with yields of 5.5-6.0 percent, and were desperately looking elsewhere for more yield. Ecu bonds and Bunds were natural candidates.
"Some investors have liabilities which are costing them more than 6.0 percent, so they are having to eat into resources. That can only persist so long," said Lindsay.
